Lying asleep walking Last night I met my father Who seemed pleased to see me. He wanted to speak. I saw His mouth saying something But the dream had no sound. We were surrounded by Laid-up paddle steamers In The Old Quay in Greenock. I smelt the tar and the ropes. It seemed that I was standing Beside the big iron cannon The tugs used to tie up to When I was a boy. I turned To see Dad standing just Across the causeway under That one lamp they keep on. He recognised me immediately. I could see that. He was The handsome, same age With his good brows as when He would take me on Sundays Saying we’ll go for a walk. Dad, what am I doing here? What is it I am doing now? Are you proud of me? Going away, I knew You wanted to tell me something. You stopped and almost turned back To say something. My father, I try to be the best In you you give me always. Lying asleep turning Round in the quay-lit dark It was my father standing As real as life. I smelt The quay’s tar and the ropes. I think he wanted to speak. But the dream had no sound. I think I must have loved him.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Lying, Last, Who

outputs.L1:
**Lying Asleep, Walking**

Last night, I met my father,  
who seemed pleased to see me.  
He wanted to speak. I saw  
his mouth forming words,  
but the dream had no sound.

We were surrounded by  
laid-up paddle steamers  
at the Old Quay in Greenock.  
I could smell the tar and the ropes.  
It seemed I was standing  
beside the great iron cannon  
where the tugs used to tie up  
when I was a boy.

I turned  
and saw Dad standing just  
across the causeway, beneath  
that one lamp they leave burning.  
He recognised me immediately—  
I could see that.

He was handsome,  
the same age as he had been,  
with those fine brows,  
when he would take me out on Sundays,  
saying, “We’ll go for a walk.”

Dad, what am I doing here?  
What is it I am doing now?  
Are you proud of me?

As I was going away, I knew  
you wanted to tell me something.  
You stopped, and almost turned back  
to speak.

My father,  
I try to be the best of you—  
the part you have always given me.

Lying asleep, turning  
in the quay-lit dark,  
it was my father standing there,  
as real as life.

I could smell  
the quay’s tar and the ropes.  
I think he wanted to speak,  
but the dream had no sound.

I think I must have loved him.
outputs.L2:
While I slept, I dreamed I was moving through the night.  
The previous evening, in that dream, I encountered my father,  
and he appeared glad that I was there.  
He seemed about to say something.  
I watched his lips form words,  
but no sound existed in the dream.

Around us were paddle steamers,  
laid aside and idle  
at the Old Quay in Greenock.  
I could smell tar, and the scent of ropes.  
I seemed to be beside the large iron cannon  
where, when I was a child,  
the tugboats used to be fastened.

I looked round  
and saw my father on the far side of the causeway,  
beneath the single lamp that is always left burning.  
At once, he knew who I was;  
I could tell that clearly.  
He looked handsome,  
as young as I remembered him,  
with the same strong brows he had  
when he used to take me out on Sundays,  
saying that we would go for a walk.

Father, why am I here?  
What am I doing with my life?  
Are you proud of me?

As I was leaving,  
I understood that there was something  
you had meant to say.  
You paused, and nearly came back,  
as if to speak.

My father,  
I try to live out the finest part of you,  
the part you have always given me.

Sleeping, turning over  
in the darkness lit by the quay,  
I saw my father there,  
as vivid as if he were alive.  
Again I smelled the tar of the quay  
and the ropes.  
I believe he wished to talk to me,  
but the dream was silent.  
I think I must have loved him.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a deeply moving dream in which the speaker imagines meeting his father again at the Old Quay in Greenock. The setting is rich with memory and atmosphere: paddle steamers, the smell of tar, thick ropes, and the familiar details of the harbour all evoke the speaker’s childhood. This place is not just a physical location, but a landscape of the past, filled with associations of family, love, and early experience.

In the dream, the father appears vividly and warmly, just as the speaker remembers him from childhood. He looks the way he did when he used to take the speaker on Sunday walks, suggesting tenderness, security, and closeness. The father’s presence is comforting and powerful, as though the dream has briefly brought him back to life. Through this image, the poem captures the intensity with which loved ones can remain alive in memory.

However, the dream is also marked by silence. The father seems as if he wants to speak, but no words are heard. This silence creates a sense of longing and loss. The speaker is given the precious sight of his father, but not the message he hopes for. The absence of speech suggests the painful separation caused by death: even in dreams, full reunion is impossible.

At the heart of the poem is the speaker’s desire for his father’s approval. He wonders whether he has lived well enough and whether his father would be proud of the person he has become. This gives the poem an emotional depth beyond simple remembrance. The speaker is not only mourning his father, but also measuring his own life against the values his father represented.

Overall, the poem expresses profound love, grief, and gratitude. It shows how strongly the father continues to shape the speaker’s identity, even after death. The speaker wants to preserve the best qualities his father gave him and to live in a way that honours his memory. The dream becomes a powerful symbol of both loss and inheritance: the father is gone, but his influence remains.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a dreamlike encounter between the speaker and his deceased father, creating an atmosphere that is both intimate and haunting. Rather than describing grief directly, the poem moves through memory, place, and sensation, allowing the father’s presence to emerge gradually. Greenock’s Old Quay becomes more than a physical setting: it is a place of return, where the speaker revisits childhood walks, family history, and moments that still carry emotional weight. The details of the landscape, the harbour, and the remembered streets help to make the past feel vivid and immediate, as though the boundary between life and death has briefly become uncertain.

At the centre of the poem is the speaker’s longing for communication with his father. The father appears, but he remains silent, and this silence becomes one of the poem’s most powerful features. It suggests everything that was left unsaid between them: affection that may not have been openly expressed, questions that can no longer be answered, and a desire for approval that still survives after death. The speaker seems to want recognition from his father, not only as a child seeking comfort but also as an adult looking back on the relationship with regret and tenderness.

The poem also explores ideas of inheritance. The father represents the speaker’s origins, values, memories, and emotional identity. Through the encounter, the speaker recognises how deeply his father has shaped him, even in absence. The remembered walks and familiar places become symbols of what has been passed down: not just family history, but ways of seeing, feeling, and belonging. The setting of Greenock’s Old Quay reinforces this sense of continuity, connecting personal memory with a wider world of work, travel, and departure.

The key emotional result of the poem is a poignant recognition of love mixed with regret. The speaker understands the strength of the bond between father and child, but that understanding comes too late for ordinary conversation. The father’s silence makes the encounter more moving because it denies the speaker the reassurance he seeks, while also suggesting a quiet, enduring presence. In this way, the poem captures the complexity of bereavement: the dead are gone, yet they remain powerfully alive in memory. Ultimately, the poem is significant because it transforms a private moment of longing into a meditation on love, loss, inheritance, and the human need for connection.
outputs.L5:
**The Last One Lying**

Who was the last one lying?

That was the question everyone asked when the truth finally came out. For days, each person had told a different version of the story. Some lied to protect themselves, others lied to protect someone they loved. But every lie left a mark, and every mark pointed back to the same night.

In the end, it was not the loudest voice or the most convincing story that mattered. It was the silence of the one person who had said the least.

Who was guilty? Who was afraid? Who had been lying from the beginning?

The answer came slowly, like the last light fading from the sky. And when it did, everyone understood that the most dangerous lie was not the one spoken aloud, but the one they had all chosen to believe.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of a 20th-century Scottish poet about dreaming of a dead father at the Old Quay in Greenock, with paddle steamers, tar, ropes, and an unsaid message.
counterfactuals.output:
At the Old Quay, Greenock,  
where the Clyde holds its breath  
under a skin of oil and pewter light,  
I dreamed my father back—

not young, not old,  
but as the dead are in dreams:  
wearing the weather of every year  
at once.

Paddle steamers nosed the grey,  
their wheels churning the river  
like memory trying to lift itself  
from silt.  
A gull cried, then thought better of it.  
Tar sweated blackly from the posts.  
Ropes lay coiled on the stones,  
thick as sleeping serpents,  
salt-stiff, tarred, ready  
for some departure already missed.

He stood by the bollards  
with his cap pulled low,  
hands in his coat pockets,  
looking not at me  
but out beyond the ferries,  
beyond Gourock,  
beyond the rain’s slow stitching  
of water to sky.

I wanted to say  
I had kept nothing properly—  
not his tools, not his stories,  
not the patience in his hands.  
I wanted to ask  
what it was he had carried  
all those years in silence,  
heavy as a hawser,  
dark as a rope-end dipped in pitch.

But the steamers called,  
deep-throated, mournful,  
and the quay trembled  
under the old commerce of leaving.

He turned then,  
as if hearing my thought  
before I had the courage of words.  
His mouth moved once.

No sound came.

Only the river,  
only the tar-smell,  
only the ropes tightening  
round the dream’s wet piles—

and the message,  
still unsaid,  
passing between us  
like a boat in fog,  
lit for a moment,  
then gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a nostalgic elegy where the speaker meets his father in a silent dream by a quay, asks whether he is proud of him, and wakes with the realization that he loved him.
counterfactuals.output:
**By the Quay**

Last night I found you where the harbor sleeps,  
beside the quay, in weathered coat and cap,  
the moon laid out in silver on the deep,  
the tide breathing softly in its lap.

No gulls cried there, no ropes knocked on the mast,  
no lantern swung, no footstep crossed the stone;  
only the water, carrying the past,  
and you, as if you had not gone.

You looked the same as in my boyhood years—  
your hands hard-earned, your silence close and kind;  
I had brought all my failures, all my fears,  
the years I could not leave behind.

I wanted to be young again, and small,  
to hear you call my name across the yard;  
instead I stood grown weary, nearly tall,  
and found the speaking strangely hard.

At last I asked, with all my courage gone,  
“Father, are you proud of me?” I said.  
The dark tide moved. The pale dream carried on.  
You only smiled and bowed your head.

Then morning broke, and you were lost once more;  
the room returned, the clock, the empty chair.  
But something warm had followed me to shore—  
a truth too plain to vanish into air:

Not every love is spoken, straight and clear.  
Some loves are harbors, quiet, deep, and wide.  
I woke, and knew what I had longed to hear:  
you loved me. You had always loved me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem about a son seeing his father as a young man in a soundless dream, set among laid-up paddle steamers and harbour lights in Greenock.
counterfactuals.output:
In a soundless dream I found him there,  
where Greenock’s harbour lights  
shook their coins across the Clyde  
and spent them on the night.  

The paddle steamers lay in rows,  
laid up, their funnels cold,  
their names half-hidden under rain,  
their brass gone dim as old  

regrets. No gull cried overhead,  
no chain complained, no bell;  
the water moved its black mouth once  
and had no tale to tell.  

And he was young beside the quay,  
before my life began,  
cap pulled low, coat collar raised—  
my father, not yet man  

to me, not yet the voice that called  
from kitchens, stairs, and years;  
not yet the hand that steadied mine  
or hid away its fears.  

He watched the silent steamers sleep,  
as if they might depart,  
as if some engine under rust  
still laboured like a heart.  

I tried to speak. My mouth shaped Dad,  
but nothing crossed the air.  
The harbour lights went trembling on;  
he did not know me there.  

Only the river seemed to know  
how time can double back—  
one shore lit up with what we lose,  
one shore already black.  

Then through the mist he turned his face,  
so young it made me grieve,  
and smiled as though he’d heard the word  
I could not make him receive.  

The steamers slept. The harbour burned.  
The dream held fast, then thinned.  
I woke with Greenock in my eyes,  
and silence in the wind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person lyric poem with plain diction and vivid dockside imagery—tar, ropes, cannon, tugs, a lamp—centered on grief, memory, and an unspoken conversation with the speaker’s father.
counterfactuals.output:
At the dock I stand where the tar  
shines black in the rain,  
where ropes lie coiled like sleeping things  
beside the old iron cleats.

A cannon faces the harbor,  
green with weather,  
mouth full of silence.  
I touch its cold side  
and think of your hands.

Tugs move out at dawn,  
low and stubborn,  
pushing the gray water aside.  
Their horns cross the bay  
like words I almost know.

Father, I do not say your name.  
I let the gulls say it badly.  
I let the lamp at the end of the pier  
burn its small gold hole  
in the fog.

You would have liked this morning—  
the smell of salt and diesel,  
the nets drying on hooks,  
the men in dark coats  
lifting crates without speech.

I have carried so much  
I never brought to you.  
Questions tied tight as rope.  
Anger hardened like pitch.  
Love, too, heavy and plain,  
too late in my mouth.

The water knocks and knocks  
against the pilings.  
It sounds like someone  
waiting to be let in.

I lean on the rail  
and answer nothing.  
Still, I hear you  
in the chain’s slow scrape,  
in the tug’s black smoke,  
in the lamp holding steady  
while everything else moves away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a tender, melancholic free verse piece beginning with “Lying asleep” and ending with the idea that the speaker must have loved his father, using a Scottish harbour setting.
counterfactuals.output:
Lying asleep  
above the harbour,  
I hear the ropes complain softly  
against their iron rings,  
the gulls crying in the haar  
as if morning were something  
they had lost.

Below, the boats nudge one another  
in the cold green water,  
names flaking from their sides—  
Morag, Saint Bride, Grace—  
and the tide lifts them  
with the patience of hands.

My father is on the pier again,  
though he has been dead for years,  
his oilskins dark with rain,  
his cap pulled low,  
a cigarette burning  
like a small red harbour light  
between his fingers.

He does not turn.  
He looks out past the mackerel clouds,  
past the lobster creels and diesel sheen,  
to where the firth opens  
its grey mouth to the North Sea.

I remember little.  
The scrape of his boots.  
Salt on his cuffs.  
The way he cleared his throat  
instead of saying anything gentle.  
A paper bag of chips  
warming my hands in the wind.

All night the tide goes out  
and comes back altered,  
bringing weed, shells,  
the blunt smell of fish,  
and somewhere in it all  
his silence,  
heavy as a net.

If grief is a boat  
I have been mending for years,  
then this morning it floats—  
not far, not bravely,  
only enough to show  
it was built for him.

And waking to rain on the window,  
to gulls and bells  
and the harbour breathing below,  
I know, with a sorrow  
almost like tenderness,  
I must have loved my father.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
